summary:
Sojourner is an interactive 3D browser game set on the surface of Mars. We built it with JavaScript, three.js, HTML, CSS, and Blender. The player explores in first person with the keyboard and mouse, following a mission briefing that says to find Sojourner, NASA’s first robotic rover to operate on another planet. Along the way, the player finds the landing platform and then the rover itself, and each discovery unlocks a new part of its story. The experience ends with a quiz that tests what the player learned.

The project addresses the challenge by turning a little-known piece of space history into something people can explore instead of read. Players learn by doing, in a short 5 to 10 minute experience that needs no prior knowledge of astronomy or robotics.

It matters because Sojourner paved the way for Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance. Telling its story in an engaging way brings space science closer to students and the general public.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Sojourner is an interactive 3D experience that runs in the browser and is set on the surface of Mars. The player explores the terrain in first person to find Sojourner, NASA’s first robotic rover to operate on another planet, and learns about its mission along the way.

  1. Start: A title screen, styled like a mission telemetry display, introduces the Mars Pathfinder mission (1997).
  2. Mission briefing: A welcome message tells the player the mission is to find Sojourner and learn about it, with a real photo of the rover on Mars.
  3. Controls: The player is taught the controls: W A S D to move, the mouse to look around, and ESC to release the cursor.
  4. Exploration: The player explores the Martian terrain. After a set stretch of exploring, the first part of the story appears on screen.
  5. Landing platform: The player is told to find the landing platform. Interacting with it unlocks another part of the story.
  6. Sojourner: The final mission is to find the rover. Reaching it unlocks the final part of the story.
  7. Quiz: The game ends with a quiz that tests what the player learned.

The code is split into small modules, each with one responsibility: player controller, interaction with objectives, progress manager, information panel, and interface (UI).

What benefits does it have?

  • Accessible: It needs no prior knowledge of astronomy or robotics.
  • Easy to access: It runs in a web browser with nothing to install, and it is designed to run smoothly on mid-range computers.
  • Quick: The experience lasts about 5 to 10 minutes.
  • Active learning: The player discovers the story by exploring instead of reading passively, and the quiz reinforces it.
  • Intuitive: The objectives appear from the start and the controls are explained before playing.
  • Expandable: More objectives, map areas, and languages can be added later.

What is the intended impact?

The goal is to tell Sojourner’s story in an immersive, entertaining way and raise awareness of its contribution to space exploration. After playing, the player should understand what Sojourner was and why it mattered. It was the first rover to operate on another planet, and it paved the way for Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance. The project targets students, space enthusiasts, and the general public. Its story is little known and usually told passively, so the project aims to bring space science closer to any audience.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML, and CSS
  • 3D library: three.js
  • Editor: Visual Studio Code
  • 3D modeling: Blender, for the terrain, rocks, Sojourner rover, and landing platform
  • Platform: Interactive web page (browser game), published on GitHub Pages
  • Content: Images, videos, and text from the mission, from NASA / JPL and the NASA Image Archive
  • Data: Static content with no database
  • Hardware: Played with a keyboard and mouse on a computer. The documentation only says it should run smoothly on mid-range machines.
  • Version control: Git, which GitHub Pages implies, although the documentation lists it as still to be defined.

How is the project creative?

  • Story through exploration: Instead of a lecture or video, the player uncovers the story by finding the landing platform and then the rover.
  • Progressive structure: The story unlocks in stages, with each objective revealing a new part.
  • Mission-control look: The interface has a telemetry style, with labels like “SYS.TELEMETRY // 1997-ARES-VALLIS” and “Mission Briefing.” It makes the player feel part of the Pathfinder mission.
  • Atmosphere: Rocky, arid terrain, reddish and orange tones, a Martian sky, dust, and scattered rocks, with a minimalist interface.
  • Sound: Ambient Martian wind and interaction sounds.
  • Ending as a challenge: The journey ends with the encounter with the rover and a quiz, under the tagline “small in size, enormous in legacy.”

What factors did the team consider?

  • Audience: The content must be understandable for non-experts.
  • Performance: The models are optimized and the view distance is limited so the 3D terrain runs well.
  • Usability: Guiding the player is a known difficulty, so the team provides clear on-screen instructions and controls from the start, and plans usability testing.
  • Time: If time runs short, the priority is movement, the objectives, and the quiz.
  • Rights: The team uses NASA resources or freely licensed material for the multimedia.
    • The rover weighed about 10.5 kg and was about 65 cm long.
    • It was solar powered and carried a spectrometer.
    • It studied rocks named Barnacle Bill and Yogi.
    • Its name honors Sojourner Truth.
    • It was designed for 7 sols but worked for more than 80, until communication was lost in September 1997.
    • Language: The game is in Spanish
